title: Why You Might Be Awake During Surgery Without Knowing It
description:
Anesthesia was supposed to be the closest thing science has to an off switch — a clean, complete erasure of the mind. But the data says something far stranger is happening.

Patients under general anesthesia have squeezed a hand on command. Some signaled pain. Almost none remembered any of it. The neurons never stopped firing — they simply stopped talking to each other.

This documentary walks through the evidence quietly reshaping what "being unconscious" means: the isolated forearm experiments, the brain that keeps listening while no one is home to hear it, and the technique that rings the brain like a bell to listen for an echo. It examines propofol, ketamine, and xenon — three drugs that look identical from the outside but leave completely different inner signatures — and the scientists asking whether the mind can be awake while the person is not.

If the brain keeps working under anesthesia, then "I was out" may describe a gap in memory, not a gap in experience. The line between asleep and awake is thinner than we've been told.

title: Daoist Phenomenology: A Vertical Reading with Dr. Jay Goulding (York University).
description:
The Following video is a special presentation of my Book series on Classical German Philosophy and Post-Kantian Thought. The title of today's episode is: Daoist Phenomenology: A Vertical Reading with Dr. Jay Goulding (York University). 

In this extra special episode of: The Young Idealist Series, I invited Dr. Jay Goulding who is an Associate Professor at York University in the Department of Equity Studies. Dr. Goulding specializes in both Chinese and Japanese philosophy, and hermeneutic phenomenology. Dr. Goulding’s main research interests are in Continental Philosophy, Classics, Wang Bi’s 王弼 reconstruction of Laozi’s 老子 Daodejing 道德經, Cheng Chung-ying’s 成中英 ontocosmology and Chinese philosophy. As well as, Hwa Yol Jung’s Daoist phenomenology, Schelling, Daoism, Heidegger’s engagement with Chinese and Japanese philosophy. 

Dr. Jay Goulding takes the viewer on a robust intellectual, spiritual, and philosophical history merging East Asian Philosophy (Chinese & Japanese thought) and Western European Continental thought. We discuss important philosophers such as Gottfried Leibniz, Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, Martin Heidegger, Hans-Georg Gadamer, Laozi, Zhuangzi, Wang Bi, Dōgen Zenji, Keiji Nishitani, & Shūzō Kuki.

Book Synopsis:

Daoist Phenomenology: A Vertical Reading
Jay Goulding
Bloomsbury 2025

"Dr. Jay Goulding’s 2025 Bloomsbury release of Daoist Phenomenology: A Vertical Reading, is a ground breaking text which features Goulding’s innovative Daoist phenomenology. In the text, East and West come together to create an original, hybrid, and organic form of phenomenology. Goulding’s book contains major and minor chapters on figures like Heidegger, Schelling, Gadamer, Merleau-Ponty, Laozi, Zhuangzi and Dōgen. 

The renowned philosopher, Dr. Jason Wirth, has described the book as Highly original and erudite … the Dao 道 emerges not as an exotic doctrine, but as the way of all Beings.”

Goulding’s Daoist Phenomenology represents a lifelong project of interpolating the works of Martin Heidegger with the interweavings of Daoism and Zen. The text Illustrates highly original and unique styles of reading complex texts from Europe and East Asia. Goulding moves away from the traditional horizontal reading methods of simple comparisons on a single plane to a vertical reading, which he describes “as a deep dive of ideas into ancient worlds.” Goulding’s Vertical Reading is a hermeneutic strategy that captures the depth of connection between phenomenology and Daoism, especially with Heidegger and classical Daoists Laozi and Zhuangzi. 

His method reveals Daoist implications of Dōgen’s Zen and draws on the writing and ideas from popular culture including; Jules Verne, H. P. Lovecraft, Philip K. Original and wide-ranging, Goulding’s interconnected approach to phenomenology and Daoism enhances and promotes further intercultural dialogues between two great traditions in world philosophies. A fascinating read for anyone who loves philosophy, phenomenology, and East Asian studies.

title: If Everyone Says Life Is Unfair, Doesn’t That Make Life Fair? ⚖️🌍
description:
Have you ever wondered why almost everyone says that life is unfair? Some people are born into wealth while others face hardship. Some work incredibly hard and still struggle, while others seem to succeed with little effort. If everyone experiences some form of unfairness, does that strange fact make life fair after all?

In this video, we explore the fascinating paradox of fairness, inequality, randomness, and our expectations about how life should work.

🔹 If everyone experiences unfairness, does that make life fair?
🔹 What does “fairness” actually mean?
🔹 Is equal treatment the same as equal outcomes?
🔹 Why do good things happen to bad people and bad things happen to good people?
🔹 Is life controlled by fairness, randomness, or something else?
🔹 Why do humans expect the universe to be fair?
🔹 Can an unfair world still contain fairness?
🔹 Does everyone having different circumstances make inequality inevitable?
🔹 Who decides what is truly fair?
🔹 Is fairness about equal opportunities or equal outcomes?

Life does not appear to follow a universal rule that guarantees everyone the same opportunities, experiences, or outcomes. Circumstances, chance, abilities, decisions, and events beyond our control can all shape the direction of our lives.

But perhaps fairness isn't about everyone receiving the same result. Maybe it is about having the same basic rules, rights, or opportunities—even when the outcomes are completely different.

And that leads to a deeper philosophical question: Are we describing life as unfair, or are we judging life against expectations that the universe never promised to satisfy?

Watch the full video to explore one of the strangest questions about fairness, inequality, and human existence: If everyone says life is unfair, doesn’t that make life fair?

title: How the License Raj Crushed Indian Entrepreneurs | Episode 9 Economic Growth Series
description:
Imagine a world where your customers want more, so you produce more. Congratulations, my friend—you have just broken the law. 🚨

This was India before 1991 under the "License Raj." A government license dictated exactly what your factory could produce.

Want to expand your factory? Ask permission.
Want to import a better machine? Ask permission.
Want to enter a new industry? Ask permission.

And then wait. Sometimes for months or even years.

This system didn't reward the entrepreneur with the best idea; it rewarded the people who could navigate the government bureaucracy. India didn't lack entrepreneurs. The government just made it nearly impossible for anyone to start a business.

The result? Fewer businesses. Less competition. Lower productivity. And a generation of Indians that had to grow up in extreme scarcity.

title: The 1991 Economic Crisis Explained | Episode 10: Economic Growth Series
description:
Last time, India had to go bankrupt before it could change.

For decades, the Indian government tried to control the economy from the centre. Many knew the system was broken. But every regulation gave someone power. So, the system survived.

Then, in 1990, Iraq invaded Kuwait. Oil prices rose. Remittances from Indians in the Gulf were disrupted. And years of excessive government borrowing had left the country drowning in debt.

When foreign lenders came to collect, India had enough foreign currency for just two weeks of imports. The crisis made reform unavoidable.

Industrial licensing was abolished for most sectors. Import duties were reduced. And the Indian market was partially opened to global competition.

But the reforms were partial. We changed many rules. But the system beneath them remains largely intact.

title: Is the Mind reducible to the Brain? | Neuroscience, Consciousness & Free Will Debate
description:
Is the mind nothing more than the product of the brain? Can consciousness, free will, and reason be fully explained by physical processes?

These are among the most important questions in contemporary neuroscience, philosophy, and biology. Research on the brain has greatly expanded our understanding of the neural basis of memory, emotions, and decision-making. Yet the problem of consciousness remains unresolved, raising the question of whether brain activity alone is sufficient to explain the human mind.

In this debate, leading scientists and scholars from different disciplines explore questions such as:

Can the mind be reduced to processes occurring in the brain?
Is consciousness merely an emergent property of neural networks?
Can neuroscience fully explain rationality, free will, and abstract thought?
Does the rise of artificial intelligence change our understanding of human cognition?
Where are the limits of scientific explanations of the mind?

This debate was organised by En Arche Foundation. It took place in Carcow, Poland on May 30th.

Speakers

Prof. Leszek Kaczmarek – Molecular biologist and neuroscientist, Full Member of the Polish Academy of Sciences, and Head of the Laboratory of Neurobiology at the Nencki Institute. His research focuses on the molecular mechanisms of brain plasticity and learning. He argues that the mind is a product of the brain, while emphasizing that it cannot be reduced simply to chemistry or isolated molecular processes.

Dr. Paweł Boguszewski – Neuroscientist and behavioral scientist at the Nencki Institute. His research examines the neural mechanisms underlying behavior and consciousness. He argues that consciousness is an emergent property of complex neural networks and that contemporary neuroscience provides no evidence for immaterial explanations.

Prof. Michael Egnor – American neurosurgeon and Professor at Stony Brook University. Drawing on neurosurgical practice and the history of neuroscience, he argues that reason and free will cannot be fully explained by brain activity alone and point toward an immaterial aspect of the human mind.

Prof. Stuart Burgess – British Professor of Mechanical Engineering, specialist in biomechanics and biomimetics, and collaborator with the European Space Agency (ESA). He presents arguments for the existence of an immaterial mind based on humanity's place in nature, our cognitive abilities, and the reality of rational thought.

title: Christopher Hitchens SHREDS John Lennox’s Case for Religious Morality
description:
Christopher Hitchens and John Lennox went head to head in Edinburgh in one of the most quoted matchups in the entire atheism versus Christianity debate archive, and this video covers the part most highlight reels skip: the closing statements, where both men finally stop talking past each other and answer each other point by point. The motion on the table was whether the new Europe should prefer the new atheism. What it turned into was a much older and much bigger question. Can a society keep morality, human dignity and meaning if it lets go of God, or is secular ethics quietly living off borrowed capital?

Christopher Hitchens was a journalist, essayist and author of God Is Not Great, and one of the four figures usually grouped together as the new atheists alongside Richard Dawkins, Sam Harris and Daniel Dennett. He spent the last decade of his life debating theologians, apologists and philosophers all over the world, and this Edinburgh appearance is one of his sharpest. John Lennox is a mathematician and Professor Emeritus at the University of Oxford who has become one of the most recognisable Christian voices in public debate. He has faced Richard Dawkins, Peter Singer and Michael Shermer, and he is known for a calm, story-driven style that plays extremely well in a live hall.

Lennox opens his close by dividing atheists into two groups. Soft atheists, in his view, quietly keep Christian values like human worth and dignity while rejecting the God those values came from. Hard atheists, he says, follow the logic all the way down. He brings in Nietzsche, Camus and Sartre, cites the ethicist Peter Singer on the moral status of infants and animals, and references the philosopher John Gray on human significance. He argues that the new atheism shares a streak of intolerance with religious fundamentalism, that lumping very different faith communities together is not an evidence-based approach, and he closes with the churches in Leipzig in 1989 and a line from Alexander Solzhenitsyn about a society that forgot God.

Hitchens answers with an epistemology question rather than a values question. What does his opponent actually know, and how does he know it? He argues that his own claims sit in the open where anyone can check or attack them, while the religious case rests on a source nobody else can access. From there he takes apart the idea of vicarious redemption, arguing that debts and prison sentences can be transferred between people but moral responsibility cannot. He raises the problem of competing religious claims, pointing out that traditions contradict each other on the details that supposedly decide eternity. And he ends with the argument now known simply as the Hitchens Challenge: name one good or noble act that a believer can perform which a non-believer cannot, then try the far easier reverse.

This debate is from 2008, and almost none of the arguments have aged. Every claim in it is still being made word for word on podcasts, campus panels and debate channels today. The structure is what makes it worth watching. There is no crossfire and no interruption, so both cases are presented at full strength, which is rare in modern debate content where everyone talks over everyone. In this reaction and breakdown I go through both closing statements from an atheist perspective, add historical context the debate itself skips over, including David Hume writing on the roots of morality in that same city centuries earlier, and explain why the final challenge is still unanswered.

Do you think real morality is possible without God? Do you find the borrowed values argument convincing, or does it fall apart under pressure? Who do you think came out on top here? Drop your answer in the comments, keep it civil, and let others make their case too. Believers and non-believers are both welcome here, and the best comment threads on this channel are the ones where people actually argue instead of just agreeing. title: What Is Legacy Software Modernization?
description:
What is legacy software modernization? It’s the process of improving an important existing software system so it can continue serving the business as technology, requirements, and risks change. And modernization does not automatically mean replacing everything or starting over.

Depending on the system, legacy software modernization might involve updating the technology stack, improving architecture, reducing technical debt, migrating infrastructure, strengthening security, improving integrations, or making future enhancements easier to deliver. The goal is to preserve what still creates value while changing what is holding the organization back.

AI is also changing what modernization projects look like. It can help engineers analyze large codebases, map dependencies, generate documentation, identify patterns, and accelerate repetitive work. That can make projects more feasible than they were in the past. Art+Logic’s current modernization practice likewise emphasizes AI-assisted code analysis and migration alongside incremental progress rather than defaulting to a full rewrite.

But legacy systems contain more than code. They also encode business rules, operational knowledge, edge cases, and years of decisions. AI can help reveal those details; experienced engineers still have to interpret what matters, decide what should change, and validate the result.

Legacy modernization isn’t about replacing the past. It’s about preparing software for what the business needs next.

These insights emphasize the importance of monitoring **muscular health** as an early indicator of future cognitive impairment.
